guidelineVersions: BSH red cell transfusion in sickle cell disease, Parts I and II (2016)

brief.scenario: Mr Samuel Okonjo, 26, has sickle cell disease (HbSS). He has had two episodes of biliary colic and is listed for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. His haemoglobin is 82 g/L.
brief.task: Answer the examiner's questions on his perioperative management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Risks, haematology plan, transfusion, right blood, avoid triggers, watch the chest.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Treating him as a routine cholecystectomy and finding out about his antibodies on the day.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd refer him to the specialist haemoglobinopathy team to plan transfusion before listing."

grid.label: Perioperative risks
grid.fail: Treats it as a routine cholecystectomy, or cannot name sickle-specific risks.
grid.pass: Acute chest syndrome, painful crisis, stroke, infection and transfusion complications; asks about previous crises, chest syndrome and transfusions.
grid.high: Links his gallstones to chronic haemolysis (pigment stones); a previous acute chest syndrome raises his risk.

grid.label: Specialist planning
grid.fail: Lists him without informing haematology or anaesthesia.
grid.pass: Early referral to the specialist haemoglobinopathy team; joint plan with the anaesthetist and haematologist before listing.
grid.high: Complex surgery belongs in a centre with specialist haemoglobinopathy support; alerts the transfusion laboratory early.

grid.label: Preoperative transfusion
grid.fail: No transfusion plan, or transfuses to a normal haemoglobin.
grid.pass: HbSS having medium-risk surgery: preoperative transfusion recommended; simple transfusion when Hb is below 90 g/L, to about 100 g/L.
grid.high: Cites TAPS: untransfused patients had more complications, mostly acute chest syndrome; exchange for high-risk surgery or severe disease.

grid.label: Blood specification
grid.fail: Requests standard crossmatched blood without telling the laboratory.
grid.pass: HbS-negative red cells matched at least for Rh (D, C, c, E, e) and K; checks his antibody history.
grid.high: Warns of delayed haemolytic reactions and hyperhaemolysis; tells the laboratory he has sickle cell disease.

grid.label: Avoiding triggers
grid.fail: Allows him to fast without IV fluids, or to become cold or hypoxic.
grid.pass: Optimises oxygenation, hydration and warmth: IV fluids while fasting, oxygen saturation monitoring, active warming, good analgesia.
grid.high: Adds early mobilisation and a clear analgesia plan, so pain after upper abdominal surgery does not stop him breathing deeply.

grid.label: Acute chest syndrome
grid.fail: Treats postoperative fever and chest pain as simple atelectasis.
grid.pass: Fever and/or respiratory symptoms with a new infiltrate on chest X-ray: oxygen, antibiotics, analgesia, incentive spirometry, urgent haematology.
grid.high: Knows severe chest syndrome needs transfusion, often exchange, and early critical care involvement.

grid.label: Emergency surgery
grid.fail: Delays an emergency operation to arrange an exchange transfusion.
grid.pass: Doesn't delay emergency surgery: simple transfusion first if Hb is below 90 g/L, provided it won't unduly delay surgery.
grid.high: If transfusion would delay surgery unacceptably, proceeds and transfuses intra- or postoperatively; haematology informed immediately.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What are the risks for him?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Same as anyone having a cholecystectomy: bleeding, bile leak, infection.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Who needs to know he's coming in?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd just put him on the list; the anaesthetist will see him on the day.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: His haemoglobin is 82. Would you transfuse?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd give three units to get him to normal.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How would you look after him on the ward?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Nil by mouth from midnight; he can drink when he's back.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Day 2 he has a fever and chest pain.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What are the risks for him?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Acute chest syndrome, painful crisis, stroke, infection and complications of transfusion. I'd ask about previous crises, chest syndrome and transfusions.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The specialist haemoglobinopathy team, early, and the anaesthetist. We'd agree a joint plan before he's listed.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: His haemoglobin is 82. Would you transfuse?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Yes. He's HbSS and this is medium-risk surgery, so preoperative transfusion is recommended: a simple top-up to about 100 g/L.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: HbS-negative red cells matched for Rh and K, and I'd check his antibody history.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How would you look after him perioperatively?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Avoid hypoxia, dehydration, cold and acidosis: IV fluids while fasting, saturation monitoring, active warming and good analgesia.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Day 2 he has a fever and chest pain.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd suspect acute chest syndrome: chest X-ray for a new infiltrate, oxygen, antibiotics, analgesia, incentive spirometry, and call haematology urgently.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What if he'd come in with acute cholecystitis needing surgery tonight?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I wouldn't delay. A simple transfusion first if Hb is below 90, as long as it doesn't unduly delay the operation.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: His gallstones are probably pigment stones from chronic haemolysis. If he's had chest syndrome before, his risk is higher.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd want him done where there's specialist haemoglobinopathy support, and I'd alert the transfusion lab now.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The TAPS trial: untransfused HbSS patients had more complications, mostly acute chest syndrome. Exchange is for high-risk surgery or severe disease.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Why tell the lab so early?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: He may have red cell antibodies. Delayed haemolytic reactions and hyperhaemolysis can be severe, so the lab needs time to find matched blood.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Upper abdominal surgery hurts to breathe through, so a clear analgesia plan and early mobilisation protect his chest.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: His saturations fall to 88% on air.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's severe chest syndrome. He may need exchange transfusion, and I'd involve critical care early.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: And if transfusing would delay the emergency operation?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Then proceed and transfuse during or after surgery, with haematology informed immediately.

failures.move: Calling postoperative fever and chest pain atelectasis.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: acute chest syndrome can progress quickly to respiratory failure.

failures.move: Ordering routine crossmatched blood without informing the laboratory.
failures.consequence: Risks alloimmunisation and delayed haemolytic reactions.
The surgical emergency progresses while waiting.

failures.move: Listing him without a haematology plan.
failures.consequence: Cancellation on the day, or surgery without transfusion.

recovery.line: Keep him oxygenated, hydrated, warm and pain-free.
Simple top-up to about 100 g/L, planned with haematology.

knowledge.fact: Preoperative transfusion is recommended for HbSS and HbSC patients having medium-risk surgery (e.g. abdominal).
Simple transfusion if Hb below 90 g/L, to a post-transfusion Hb of 100 g/L; consider exchange for high-risk surgery.
In TAPS, clinically important complications were 39% without and 15% with preoperative transfusion.
Blood should be HbS-negative and matched at least for Rh (D, C, c, E, e) and K.
Acute chest syndrome: fever and/or respiratory symptoms with a new infiltrate on chest X-ray.

recall.think: Acute chest syndrome, crisis and stroke; transfusion reactions.
recall.say: "I'd plan his transfusion with the haemoglobinopathy team."
do: Top-up transfusion; HbS-negative, Rh and K matched

numbers.meaning: target Hb after simple preoperative transfusion

recall.trap: Postoperative fever and chest pain are not always atelectasis.
recall.finish: Transfused, warm, hydrated and oxygenated; chest watched closely after surgery.

sources.name: Davis BA, Allard S, Qureshi A, et al; British Society for Haematology. Guidelines on red cell transfusion in sickle cell disease Part II: indications for transfusion. Br J Haematol 2017;176:192–209
sources.supports: Preoperative transfusion recommended for SS and SC patients having medium-risk surgery (e.g. abdominal); simple transfusion if Hb <90 g/L to 100 g/L; exchange for high-risk surgery or severe disease; optimise oxygenation, hydration and warmth; close liaison with haematology; complex surgery in centres with specialist support; emergency surgery: simple transfusion if Hb <90 g/L without undue delay, otherwise transfuse intra- or postoperatively

sources.name: Davis BA, Allard S, Qureshi A, et al; British Society for Haematology. Guidelines on red cell transfusion in sickle cell disease. Part I: principles and laboratory aspects. Br J Haematol 2017;176:179–91
sources.supports: Red cells HbS-negative and matched at least for Rh (D, C, c, E, e) and K; alloimmunisation, delayed haemolytic reactions and hyperhaemolysis

sources.name: Howard J, Malfroy M, Llewelyn C, et al. The Transfusion Alternatives Preoperatively in Sickle Cell Disease (TAPS) study: a randomised, controlled, multicentre clinical trial. Lancet 2013;381:930–8
sources.supports: Clinically important complications 39% without vs 15% with preoperative transfusion; most serious adverse events were acute chest syndrome

sources.name: Howard J, Hart N, Roberts-Harewood M, et al; BCSH Committee. Guideline on the management of acute chest syndrome in sickle cell disease. Br J Haematol 2015;169:492–505
sources.supports: Definition of acute chest syndrome; oxygen, antibiotics, analgesia, incentive spirometry; transfusion and critical care in severe cases

sources.name: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery (O'Connell, McCaskie, Sayers, eds)
sources.supports: Pigment gallstones in chronic haemolysis; perioperative complications of sickle cell disease

partner.opening: Mr Okonjo has HbSS disease and is listed for laparoscopic cholecystectomy. What are the risks for him?

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about his sickle history
reveals.finding: Two or three painful crises a year. One episode of acute chest syndrome two years ago needing ICU. Transfused twice.
Laboratory record: anti-E antibody detected after his last transfusion.
Temperature 38.4°C, RR 26, SpO2 91% on air, pleuritic chest pain. New left basal shadowing on chest X-ray.

push.question: Would you transfuse him before surgery?
push.expect: Yes: HbSS, medium-risk surgery; simple transfusion to about 100 g/L.

push.question: What blood would you ask for?
push.expect: HbS-negative, Rh and K matched; account for his anti-E.

push.question: What is acute chest syndrome?
push.expect: Fever and/or respiratory symptoms with a new infiltrate on chest X-ray.

curveballs.prompt: He has anti-E from a previous transfusion.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Tell the laboratory now; they need time to find E-negative, Rh and K matched blood.

curveballs.prompt: He presents instead with acute cholecystitis and needs surgery tonight.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Don't delay; simple transfusion if Hb below 90 g/L without undue delay; haematology informed.

curveballs.prompt: His saturations fall to 88% on air on day 2.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Severe acute chest syndrome: oxygen, urgent haematology, transfusion (often exchange) and critical care.
